sections.h: 'Truly' in the flesh: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1-7
sections.b: The first seven chapters of Ignatius's letter to Smyrna defend Christ's real humanity at length. He gives glory to 'Jesus Christ, the God' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1) and in the same breath confesses that he is 'truly of David's family according to the flesh', 'truly born of a virgin', baptized by John, and 'truly nailed for us in the flesh' under Pontius Pilate and Herod (1:1-2). He 'truly suffered, just as he also truly raised himself' (2:1), and was 'in the flesh even after the resurrection', eating and drinking with the disciples (3:1-3). Christ is 'flesh-bearing' (5:2), 'the perfect human being' (4:2), and the church's thanksgiving 'is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins' (7:1). Against those who said it all only seemed so, Ignatius argues from his own chains: if Christ suffered only in appearance, 'then I too am in chains only in appearance' (4:2). See also the page Docetism.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:1-3; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1; Romans 1:3; 1 John 4:2

sections.h: Smyrna: 'they themselves are only in appearance'
sections.b: Ignatius's letter to the church at Smyrna answers the teaching at length. Some 'say, that he suffered only in appearance'; 'They themselves are only in appearance!' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1). He does not name them (5:3), calls them 'beasts in human form' whom the church should avoid but pray for (4:1), says they deny that Christ was 'flesh-bearing' (5:2), that they 'do not care about love' for widows, orphans, prisoners and the hungry (6:2), and that they 'keep away from the thanksgiving and from prayer, because they do not confess that the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ' (7:1). Lightfoot inferred from 8:1 that they held a meal of their own apart from the church. Whether they were the same people as the Judaizers of Ignatius's other letters, Lake says, 'is disputed'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:1-3; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1

sections.h: Smyrna: the thanksgiving, the love feast and the overseer
sections.b: Ignatius's letter to Smyrna has two sentences on the Supper that the churches still quote. Of the teachers who denied Christ's real body: 'They keep away from the thanksgiving and from prayer, because they do not confess that the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised in his kindness' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1). And: 'Count that thanksgiving valid which is under the overseer, or under someone he entrusts it to' (8:1); 'It is not lawful to baptize or to hold a love feast without the overseer' (8:2). Lightfoot thought the love feast still included the thanksgiving, as at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:17-34); Lake notes that some scholars doubt it. Catholic teaching quotes 8:1 (Catechism 1369). The card at chapter 8 asks who may lead the Supper and baptize; Christ's presence in the bread is the card at Matthew 26:26.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1-2; 1 Corinthians 11:17-34; Jude 1:12; Matthew 26:26-28

sections.b: 'Wherever the overseer appears, there let the people be, just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2). The Catholic Encyclopedia and the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod both call this the first use of the phrase. Lightfoot: here it means 'the general or universal Church, as opposed to a particular body of Christians'; the later sense, the church 'as opposed to the heretical sects', came after. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes the line for the meaning of 'catholic' (Catechism 830).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2; Matthew 18:20; Ephesians 1:22-23

sections.h: Overseer, council of elders, deacons at Smyrna
sections.b: Ignatius tells the Smyrnaeans: 'follow the overseer the way Jesus Christ follows the Father. Follow the council of elders as if it were the apostles. Respect the deacons as God's command' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1), and greets the three in that order (12:2). Here one overseer leads the city's church, unlike the New Testament's overseers and elders who seem to be one group (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7). See the cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 9:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:2; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Philippians 1:1

sections.h: Deacons in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans
sections.b: 'Respect the deacons as God's command' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1). Ignatius calls them 'my fellow slaves' (12:2), welcomes Philo and Rheus Agathopus 'as deacons of God' (10:1), and writes by Burrhus, an Ephesian deacon and 'a model of service to God' (12:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1-2

sections.h: 'As if it were the apostles' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1)
sections.b: Ignatius compares the overseer to Jesus Christ and the council of elders to the apostles (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1). He uses the picture of a local church, not a chain of ordinations, and he does not speak of succession here. Catholic teaching quotes his rule on the valid thanksgiving under the bishop (Catechism 1369). See the card at 2 Timothy 2:2.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1; 2 Timothy 2:2; Acts 1:20-26

sections.h: Not without the overseer (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2)
sections.b: 'It is not lawful to baptize or to hold a love feast without the overseer' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2). Ignatius does not speak of emergencies. The Catholic Catechism today names the bishop, priest and (in the Latin Church) deacon as the 'ordinary ministers' but allows that 'In case of necessity, any person, even someone not baptized, can baptize' (Catechism 1256); the Westminster Confession says baptism may be dispensed only 'by a minister of the Word lawfully ordained' (27.4). See the card on Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2; Matthew 28:19

sections.h: 'Take hold, feel me and see' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3)
sections.b: 'I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:1). The risen Christ said to 'those with Peter', 'Take hold, feel me and see that I am not a bodiless demon', and 'he ate and drank with them as a man of flesh, though in spirit he was united with the Father' (3:2-3). The saying is close to Luke 24:39 in sense, not words; Eusebius did not know its source, Jerome gave it to the Gospel according to the Hebrews, and Origen knew it from a 'Teaching of Peter' (Lightfoot).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:1-3; Luke 24:36-43; Acts 10:41; John 20:27

sections.b: Ignatius ties Christ's real death and rising to ours: 'he truly suffered, just as he also truly raised himself' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1); the teachers should repent and come back 'to the suffering, which is our resurrection' (5:3); it would be better for them 'to love, so that they might also rise' (7:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:3; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1; 1 Corinthians 15:12-22

sections.b: Ignatius's word for Christ is 'flesh-bearing' (sarkophoros): whoever does not confess it 'is himself a carrier of a corpse' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:2). He greets the church 'in his flesh and blood ... of the flesh and of the spirit' (12:2), his pair for the whole of Christian life (3:2; 13:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:2; 1 John 4:2

sections.b: In Ignatius's confession at Smyrna, Christ is 'truly of David's family according to the flesh, and Son of God by the will and power of God. He was truly born of a virgin' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1). The word 'truly' answers those who made his human life an appearance (2:1). See also Ignatius to the Ephesians 18-19.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1; Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-35

sections.h: Baptized 'so that by him all righteousness might be fulfilled'
sections.b: Ignatius includes Jesus's baptism by John in his confession, with the reason given only in Matthew 3:15: 'baptized by John so that by him all righteousness might be fulfilled' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1). Lightfoot: 'Nothing is said respecting the motive of Jesus in coming to baptism in the other Canonical Gospels.'
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1; Matthew 3:13-17

sections.h: 'Under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch'
sections.b: Ignatius fixes the crucifixion in history: 'Under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch he was truly nailed for us in the flesh' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2), naming the two rulers together as Acts 4:27 does.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2; Acts 4:27; Luke 23:6-12; 1 Timothy 6:13

sections.b: 'Herod the tetrarch', Herod Antipas, stands beside Pilate in Ignatius's confession (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2), as in Luke 23:6-12 and Acts 4:27.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2; Luke 3:1; Luke 23:6-12

sections.b: 'Even the things in heaven, the glory of the angels, and the rulers seen and unseen, if they do not believe in the blood of Christ, will face judgment too' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:1), in the language of Colossians 1:16.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:1; Colossians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 6:3

sections.b: Ignatius charges the false teachers with caring nothing 'for the widow, not for the orphan, not for the oppressed' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2), and greets 'the virgins who are called widows' (13:1). Lightfoot rejected the common view that the order of widows included unmarried virgins and read the phrase as 'those women whom, though by name and in outward condition they are widows, I prefer to call virgins'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16; James 1:27

sections.b: Ignatius's test of false belief at Smyrna is neglect of the poor: 'They do not care about love: not for the widow, not for the orphan, not for the oppressed, not for the one in chains or the one set free, not for the hungry or the thirsty' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2; Matthew 25:35-36; 1 John 3:17

sections.b: Ignatius warns Smyrna against 'beasts in human form': 'You must not only refuse to receive them; if you can, do not even meet them. Only pray for them, in case they may somehow repent' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:1). He will not write their names (5:3) and calls them those who 'hold other opinions' (6:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:1-3; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:2; 2 John 10-11

sections.b: Ignatius gives a saying of the risen Jesus found in no Gospel: 'Take hold, feel me and see that I am not a bodiless demon' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:2). Eusebius did not know where it came from; Jerome said it was in the Gospel according to the Hebrews; Origen knew 'I am not a bodiless demon' from a book called the Teaching of Peter (as Lightfoot quotes them). It is close in sense to Luke 24:39.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:2; Luke 24:39

sections.b: From Troas Ignatius wrote to the church at Smyrna, where he had stayed (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1). It had an overseer, a council of elders and deacons (12:2), households, widows (13:1), and members he names: Tavia, Alce, Daphnus, Eutecnus (13:2). Lightfoot thought Alce might be the Alce whose brother Nicetes appears at Polycarp's death (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:0; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1-2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:1-2; Revelation 2:8-11

sections.h: Peace at Antioch (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11)
sections.b: At Troas news came that the church at Antioch was at peace. Ignatius asks the Smyrnaeans to 'elect an envoy of God' to go to Syria and rejoice with them that 'their own body has been restored to them' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1-3

sections.b: Ignatius greets the Smyrnaeans' 'overseer, worthy of God' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:2) without naming him. His companion letter To Polycarp is addressed to 'Polycarp, overseer of the church of the Smyrnaeans', and Eusebius calls Polycarp the one 'who led it' (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:2

sections.b: Written from Troas by Burrhus (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1), the letter defends Christ's real flesh against teachers who said he suffered 'only in appearance' (2:1), uses the phrase 'the catholic church' (8:2), which the Catholic Encyclopedia calls its first use, and asks Smyrna to send an envoy to Antioch (11:2). A fifth-century papyrus at Berlin holds 3:3-12:1 (Lake).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1
